items.title: 8Ball & MJG – On The Outside Looking In
items.author: deedub77
items.content:
On their 1993 debut album (which, at nine tracks, felt more like an EP), 8Ball & MJG made quite an impression. The duo used their debut (and the Suave House label’s inaugural album) to spew brash bars filled with gangsta/player/pimp Memphis theology over Tony Draper’s lo-fi but funky production. The shit was pretty damn entertaining and more than lived up to its name. 8Ball & MJG would return in ‘94, looking to build on their debut’s momentum with their sophomore effort, .

The founder and CEO of Suave House, Tony Draper, was credited with producing all of . For , 8Ball & MJG, along with South O, are credited with the production. track count is lengthier than ‘s, coming in at a healthy fifteen, and the duo invited a few guests to join them on a couple of records. is the first of two 8Ball & MJG albums distributed by Relativity Records. But even with Relativity’s support, the album failed to reach gold status (unlike the unofficial hood gold certification received).

Hey. Some of my favorite hip-hop albums don’t have a gold certification. I’m still excited to look into this album from the outside.

– Over slick background music suitable for a pimp’s conversation, 8Ball & MJG casually talk on the phone about finishing the album. It wasn’t a necessary intro, but I’ve heard far more useless ones.

– The team creates a dark and mystic atmosphere (I’m pretty sure I hear sprinkled elements of “Nautilus” in the track) for 8Ball and MJG to grip their nuts and talk their gangsta shit, and the duo sounds convincing. Papa Reu stops by to add a little raspy dancehall chant to the hook, making the opening record sound even more menacing.

– Slick, slippery production (complete with irresistible, whiny West Coast synth chords) that the Memphis duo slides all over, especially 8Ball. This track is complete flames. Easily one of my favorite records on the album.

– Single-handedly, Dr. Dre has sampled “(Not Just) Knee Deep” and “Atomic Dog” enough to satisfy hip-hop’s eternal quota, even before 1994. So you can only imagine how excited I was to hear 8Ball & MJG spit generic party rhymes over unimaginative flips of both loops. This is the first dud on .

– Now that’s a convoluted song title for a weed record. The late MC Breed joins our hosts as the trio transforms into the Sesshead Funk Brothers (according to MJG) and raps about their collective love for Mary Jane over obscure seventies funk. This was a fun, funky, feel-good record. But I’m sure Snoop wouldn’t agree with 8Ball’s claims of being the god of smoke or the almighty chiefa.

– The backdrop features “Inner City Blues”-like instrumentation over Fred Wesley drums, while Rodney Ellis does his best Marvin Gaye impersonation on the hook. 8 & M get a little introspective as they discuss maintaining, despite living in a crooked system designed to make them fail. 8Ball’s depthful first verse might be the best one spat on the entire album.

– Sticking with the Marvin Gaye theme, this sleek instrumental borrows from Marvin Gaye’s “I Want You.” 8 and M vow to stay ten toes down in the booth, streets, and life in general. This was tough; easily one of the best records on the album.

– The song title might lead you to believe our hosts are going to share a day in the life of 8Ball & MJG. Instead, they reminisce about their childhood, early street hustles, and getting into the rap game. The rhymes were solid, but Rick James’ “Mary Jane” is another sample that should be hung in the hip-hop rafters and never used for anotha hip-hop song.

– 8Ball gets the first solo joint of the evening. He spits a “true tale” that also works as a PSA about the consequences of living a life of crime, which he sums up as a “one-way road” to prison. Rapping from the criminal’s perspective keeps 8 from sounding preachy, and the solemn interpolated pieces from Isaac Hayes’ classic “Walk On By” give his one-verse wonder more validity.

On Tha Outside Lookin’ In – The title track is a two-minute, one-verse MJG solo record, rapped from the perspective of an incarcerated hustler. It’s decent, but why the hell did they spell the album title correctly and the song title Ebonically? It might be a small discrepancy to you, but I find the inconsistency annoying as shit.

– Well, they almost made it through an entire album without a misogyny track. But compared to the egregiousness of “Pimps” and “Niggas Like Us” on (which found 8Ball obsessed with “beatin’ up bitches”), this one almost feels wholesome. 8Ball made me chuckle a few times during the track, but overall, I wasn’t entertained.

– Our hosts invite a few friends (Thorough and Crime Boss) to join them for this album-closing cipher session. Some Memphis hip-hop historians call this record a foundational piece of the Crunk movement that consumed hip-hop in the late nineties to early 2000s, mainly for its high-energy hook. I can rock with that theory.

On “No Sellout,” 8Ball raps, “In ‘93 I was rappin’ about my curls and my Cadillac, the pimp blast, takin’ you fast, smokin’ grass and all that.” He follows those bars with “Players got the message, busters didn’t attempt to listen, thinkin’ that we was talkin’ about that on the-corner-fake-pimpin’.” Well, I beg your pardon, Mr. Ball, but I won’t allow you to insult my intelligence. I did listen to (which was released in ’93), from beginning to end several times over. You and MJG were clearly rapping about that “on-the-corner-fake-pimpin'” amongst other ignorant hood shit during the album’s nine-track runtime. The project was riddled with stories of violence, crime, and pimpin’, and all of the content was blunt and direct (sometimes uncomfortably blunt and direct) with no room left for abstract interpretation. I still enjoyed it, though. But I also enjoy seeing rappers show growth, which is what 8Ball & MJG do on On The Outside Looking In.

8Ball and MJG don’t completely abandon the ratchetness that flooded . The misogyny is significantly toned down and approached more playfully on tracks like “Players Night Out” and “Break-A-Bitch College,” compared to the harsh tone of “Pimps” and “Niggas Like Us.” They provide a decent amount of tough guy talk (see “Lick ‘Em Up Shot,” “Crumbz 2 Brixx,” and “Lay It Down”), but tracks like “So What U Sayin’,” “No Sellout,” and “No Mercy” bring a level of consciousness to that didn’t exist on . It’s not Public Enemy or Boogie Down Productions levels of consciousness, but enough consciousness to bring a righteous balance to the album’s ratchetness. And while we’re speaking of balance, 8Ball and MJG may have been equally yoked lyrically on , but 8Ball is noticeably nicer with the bars than his counterpart on .

As I mentioned at the beginning of this post, the Tony Draper-orchestrated production on had a low-budget feel. But the economical sonics felt soulful and kept my head bobbin’ for the most part. The instrumentals on are cleaner, crisper, and more developed than its predecessor; so what production lacks in soul, it compensates for with quality.

The American businessman/poet Samuel Ullman once said: “Maturity is the ability to think, speak, and act your feelings within the bounds of dignity.” I may have enjoyed a little bit more than for the organically raw feel of the production. But their sophomore effort is a more dignified musical expression and a solid second outing from the Memphis tandem.

-DeedubFollow me on Instagram @damontimeisillmatic
